messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mereana, a 71-year-old Māori woman, had spent most of her adult life working as a police officer, and the event she now returns to in fragments happened during one late shift that still feels, to her, like it split life into before and after. She had been called to a serious road crash, and when she arrived the scene was chaotic: twisted metal, people shouting, and one injured child’s mother nearby, reeking of alcohol, trying to explain what had happened through tears and panic. The child was alive but badly hurt, and Mereana was left with the unbearable certainty that something had gone wrong under her watch. In the months that followed, she began to replay that night in a way that made the images feel almost physical. Her memories were not like a story she could tell from beginning to end; they came as vivid pictures, sharp and detailed, and sometimes with sounds intruding in her head as if she were back there hearing the noise of the crash, the cries, and the frantic voices around her.

What brought those memories back most strongly were ordinary moments that now felt contaminated by the scene. Seeing cars hit in an accident, even briefly on the roadside or on television, could stop her in her tracks. Talk about accidents was no easier; if someone at work started discussing a collision, she would feel her body tense before she had fully registered what was being said. The smell of alcohol was particularly hard to bear. In a supermarket aisle, at a family gathering, or when a stranger passed by with alcohol on their breath, she would be pulled straight into the same images and sounds from that night. Those reminders did not just upset her; they confirmed what she had come to believe about herself. Each time a crash image, an accident discussion, or the smell of alcohol set off the scene again, she was driven back to the thought that the event happened because of the way she acted, that she should have protected others and failed, and that she could not stop bad things from happening to her or to people she was meant to keep safe.

Over time, Mereana began to organize her life around avoiding those reminders. She was still married, but at home she would change the channel if an accident came on the news and would leave the room if family members started talking about road injuries. At work, the avoidance was harder to hide. Although she remained employed as a police officer, she started maneuvering away from tasks that might expose her to collision scenes or long conversations about crashes, and she noticed herself becoming more guarded during shifts. The problem was that the very things she worked so hard to avoid kept appearing in the life she had built: on patrol, at roadside incidents, in everyday conversations with colleagues, and in the public spaces she used to move through without thinking. Each encounter seemed to bring back the same detailed pictures and the same sounds, and each return made her more certain that she had failed in some basic way. She began to feel that if she had acted differently at that crash, she might have prevented the harm, and when she could not shake the images, she took that as further proof that she had not done enough.

In the second half of this pattern, the loop tightened. The more often Mereana was jolted by accident imagery or the smell of alcohol, the more firmly she settled into blame and helplessness. She would leave a conversation abruptly, then spend the rest of the evening replaying the event in sharp fragments, hearing the sounds inside her head and seeing the scene as clearly as if it were happening again. That replay made her dread the next reminder, and the dread made her scan constantly for anything that might signal a crash or a discussion of one. It was exhausting, and it eroded her confidence in both her work and her role in the family. She came to intake because the pattern had become impossible to keep managing alone: she was still carrying the weight of the child’s injury, still ashamed that she had not prevented it, and increasingly afraid that one more unexpected reminder would leave her unable to function at all. What she most hoped for was relief from the images and the sounds, and what she most feared was that she would remain forever the person who failed when it mattered most.
